name: Bitcoin Trail
description:
A network capture was recovered from a system suspected of conducting an unauthorized cryptocurrency transaction.

Your mission is to analyze the provided PCAP file and trace the network communication to identify the Bitcoin wallet address involved in the transaction.

name: EMBEDDED TEXT
description:
The image appears ordinary at first glance.

However, the analyst suspects that someone has concealed additional information inside the file. The visible image may only be the surface — something else is embedded within it.

Your task is to examine the image and recover the hidden text.

🎯 Mission

Analyze embedded-text.jpg and extract the hidden payload.
Recover the concealed text and submit it as the flag.

Suggested Tools

strings
exiftool
binwalk

🚩 Flag Format

name: HIDDEN
description:
Something unusual has been found inside the Windows System32 directory.
The file appears to be an ordinary .dll, and its name suggests that it should perform a particular function. But appearances can be misleading.
Investigate the file carefully. There may be something attached to it that isn't visible through a normal file listing.

🎯 Mission
Analyze the suspicious DLL and uncover the hidden data associated with the file.
Recover the concealed flag.

🛠️ Suggested Tools
Windows Command Prompt
PowerShell
dir
streams
NTFS Alternate Data Stream (ADS) analysis tools

🚩 Flag Format
Submit the recovered flag using the traditional format:
pcgCTF{theflaghere}

name: HIT A BRICK WALL
description:
The spare key is usually under the doormat, hidden inside a plant pot, or tucked beneath a rock.
But this time, there is no key waiting in any of those places.
There is a wall.
And someone left something behind on it.

🎯 Mission
Investigate the provided artifact and uncover the hidden message.
The clue may be hiding in the writing itself.
You are looking for a traditional flag{}.

🛠️ Suggested Tools
strings
Hex editor
Text/encoding analysis tools
Steganography tools

🚩 Flag Format
Submit the recovered flag using the traditional format:
pcgCTF{theflaghere.......}

hints.content: Sometimes the most important clue is right in front of you.
Don't just look at the surroundings — examine what has been written.
The writing is on the wall.
Pay attention to how the information is represented, not just what it appears to say.

name: TURTLES ALL THE WAY DOWN
description:
At first glance, this appears to be nothing more than an archive filled with pictures of happy turtles.
But one of them doesn't belong.
Somewhere among the collection is a turtle that isn't quite as happy as the others. The original image may also hold an important clue about what has been changed.
Find the unusual image and uncover what has been hidden.
You are looking for a traditional flag{}.

🎯 Mission
Investigate the collection of turtle images, identify the unusual image, and recover the hidden flag.
Pay particular attention to the dimensions and visual structure of the images.

🛠️ Suggested Tools
file
ImageMagick
ExifTool
Python/PIL
Image viewer
Steganography analysis tools
🚩 Flag Format

Submit the recovered flag using the traditional format:

pcgCTF{theflaghere}

hints.content: Most of the turtles are happy. One isn't.
Compare the images rather than examining them individually.
Image dimensions can reveal something unusual.
The original image was a square.
Look for an image whose current dimensions don't match what you would expect.

name: EASY PACKET 1  The Exposed Request
description:
A network capture has been recovered from a suspicious communication session.

Download EASY PACKET 1.pcap and investigate it in Wireshark. Examine the Ethernet, IPv4, TCP, and HTTP layers. Pay particular attention to the HTTP request headers and the Authorization field.

OBJECTIVE: Recover the credentials exposed in the captured HTTP Basic Authentication request and submit them in the format pcgCTF{flagheree}.

HINT: Basic Authentication encodes credentials with Base64. Look for an Authorization header inside the HTTP request.

hints.content: Basic Authentication encodes credentials with Base64. Look for an Authorization header inside the HTTP request.

hints.content: HINT: Expand Internet Protocol Version 4.

hints.content: HINT: Inspect the Header Length (IHL) field.

hints.content: HINT: Find Total Length in the IPv4 header.

name: EASY PACKET 1 #09  Packet Identity

hints.content: HINT: Inspect the Identification field in the IPv4 header.

EASY PACKET 1 #26  Identify the Client

hints.content: HINT: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Identify the exposure and the secure transport that provides TLS.

name: PCGCTF Juice Shop Gateway
description:
Description

Welcome to the PCGCTF OWASP Juice Shop Laboratory.

This challenge is part of the PCGCTF Juice Shop Challenge Track.

All challenges belonging to the OWASP Juice Shop track are identified with the tag PCGCTF-JuiceShop-Challenges.

This challenge requires a local OWASP Juice Shop instance running on your machine.

The following files are provided with this challenge:

docker-compose.yml — Docker configuration for deploying the PCGCTF Juice Shop instance.
PLAYER_SETUP.txt — Instructions for installing Docker, configuring the Juice Shop, setting the required CTF_KEY, and starting the application.

Complete the environment setup before beginning the challenge.

Target

Once the Juice Shop is running, access:

http://localhost:3000
Objective

Perform basic reconnaissance against your assigned Juice Shop instance.

Your first task is to locate the hidden Score Board within the application.

Investigate the web application and identify information that is intentionally exposed but not immediately visible from the main page.

The Score Board contains the information required to complete this challenge.

Mission

Find the hidden Score Board and obtain the flag associated with this challenge.

Submit the recovered flag to CTFd.

Flag Format
pcgCTF{...}


Unlock Condition

Prerequisite: None

Successfully solving PCGCTF Gateway will unlock the next challenge in the progression.

name: BAD BLOCKCHAIN
description:
A newly discovered botnet has been using the Bitcoin blockchain as a backup communication channel.

Instead of placing its command-and-control information in the familiar OP_RETURN field, the malware authors used another part of the Bitcoin transaction data to conceal an IP address.
Investigators recovered the Bitcoin address and two associated transactions, but the actual C2 address is still hidden somewhere in the blockchain data.
Your task is to uncover the hidden IP address.
Note: The answer is an IP address.

🎯 Mission
Analyze the Bitcoin transactions associated with the provided address and identify the hidden IP address being used as the botnet's backup command-and-control server.

📁 Evidence
Bitcoin Address
1CTFzzCwntEm3a6CBGBfgxZdiArwY1HBSD

Bitcoin Transactions
4a616f943720325cc87611bf4a3bbcf2b5071baf5aab9a0ffbb9297371377c41
27bf9358822ef3ae44391950379e9206319e3bb3866d44bd9595a0e7cbdc2ca8

Blockchain API
https://api.blockcypher.com/v1/btc/main/addrs/1CTFzzCwntEm3a6CBGBfgxZdiArwY1HBSD?limit=2&before=696257

The address contains two confirmed transactions corresponding to block heights 696255 and 696256.

hints.content: The information is not stored using the usual OP_RETURN technique.
Examine the complete transaction structure rather than looking only at the address balance.
Bitcoin transactions contain several fields that can carry data.
Pay close attention to unusual or unexpected values within the transaction.
The hidden value represents an IPv4 address.

name: Ghost of Squares Past
description:
Intelligence gathered from DEADFACE communications suggests that the group has been using Savannah, Georgia's historic squares to conceal a coded message. Investigators recovered five clues, a combination of riddles and photographs, each pointing to a specific location within the city's historic district.

DEADFACE appears to have arranged these locations into a compass pattern, with the first four representing North, East, South, and West, and the fifth marking the center.

Your mission is to identify all five locations and reconstruct the hidden message before DEADFACE can put it to use.

For the first four locations, determine the year each square was established. For the final location, identify the surname engraved on its monument.

Flag Format: Deadface{YEAR-YEAR-YEAR-YEAR-SURNAME}

Submit your findings in the order provided by the clues. The flag is the year each square was discovered and the name etched into the 5th point. All in order.

Point 1 - Riddle
First of them all, where the city began, A banker's green heart in Oglethorpe's plan. A Quaker from Rhode Island sleeps under stone here Mark the year this first square was laid out, and draw near.

Point 2 - Location
Point 2

Point 3 - Riddle
Riddle Just a ways away a battle of a northern frontier Gave its name to this ground eighteen-twelve drawing near. Where a feather once drifted and a founder stands tall, Mark the year it was laid out, the newest of all.

Point 4 - Location
Point 4

Point 5 - Riddle
Four points now marked, good work, you did your best Their meeting point holds the key to this test. Carry their years in that order, and seek the lone name Carved in the stone where their center lays claim.

Submit the flag as: deadface{YYYY-YYYY-YYYY-YYYY-surname}. Example: deadface{1990-1982-1956-1985-smith}.

name: Bedside Manner
description:
DEADFACE is taking credit for an attack that compromised patient data at St Dymphna's Medical Center. Somehow, DEADFACE acquired sensitive patient records from the medical center that used the device. Funny thing is, the device that housed the data is internal without access to the internet. Which means DEADFACE would have had to have physically infiltrated the medical center!

The medical center sent us security camera footage of two individuals who told staff they were with IT, but when we asked the IT department, they said they have no idea who they were.

We're giving you access to the device we believe was compromised. We're asking you to conduct a medical device penetration test on the machine to identify vulnerabilities so we can determine if (and how) the device was compromised.

Your first task is to identify any lingering strings developer's may have left in the device's kiosk web browser.

[Access the Device](http://emedra.dctf.io:8080/)

But museum officials have received intelligence suggesting that DEADFACE infiltrated the gallery during the exhibition and secretly replaced one of the original paintings with a forgery.

All five paintings were scanned and entered into the museum's digital archive upon their return. Although the artwork appears authentic, investigators suspect that the forger left behind traces of their work in the digital records.

The museum has provided copies of all five images and needs your help identifying the compromised artwork.

Can you determine which painting was forged and recover the flag left behind?

Submit the flag as deadface{flag-text}.

name: CryptoMaze
description:
A hidden flag has been protected using two layers of cryptography.

First, a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) is used to derive the key. The resulting key is then used with AES encryption to protect the flag.

Your mission is to reverse the process, reconstruct the LFSR output, derive the AES key, and decrypt the encrypted flag.

🎯 Mission

Recover the original flag from the encrypted data.

📁 Evidence

Download the encrypted flag file provided with this challenge.

The file contains:

The initial LFSR state
The LFSR taps
The encrypted flag in hexadecimal format

🧠 Objectives
Understand the provided LFSR configuration.
Reconstruct the LFSR sequence.
Derive the AES key from the generated output.
Use the derived key to decrypt the encrypted flag.
Submit the recovered flag.
🛠️ Recommended Tools
Python
A cryptography library such as PyCryptodome
Hexadecimal analysis tools

🚩 Flag Format
FLAG:pcgCTF{scrambledeggg..}


Analyst Note: This challenge is designed to test your ability to reverse a custom key-generation process and apply cryptographic reasoning to recover protected data.

name: Info Leaks
description:
Created By: @G2Gh0st

Aurora Health has been dealing with a wave of highly targeted phishing attacks against its patients. The messages are convincing, contain accurate patient information, and are resulting in an alarming number of successful compromises.

Investigators have identified one common link among the victims: every affected patient recently installed Aurora Health's new Patient Portal iOS application. Security analysts suspect the app may be exposing sensitive information that DEADFACE is using to craft its phishing campaigns. We have been given a copy of the application for analysis. Fully evaluate the app and determine what information is being leaked so we can truly identify the source of the exposure before more patients fall victim to the attacks.

Your first task is to determine the patient's name and DOB for the patient that last used this specific version of the app. Submit the data as the flag in this format: deadface{firstname-lastname-YYYY-MM-DD}

name: Second Opinion
description:
On the touchscreen, the current patient is redacted to initials and a masked record number. Even without a login, it might be possible to determine sensitive information about the patient. There are ports available on the device that are used for maintenance, but they're not locked or concealed with a plate. See if you can find information by using a tool from your toolkit.

Submit the flag as deadface{flag-text}.

[Access the Device](http://emedra.dctf.io:8080/)

name: Hard Kept Secrets
description:
De Monne Financial has had several security incidents revolving around the latest version of their Android mobile application. Sensitive user data is being compromised left and right. De Monne is unsure how DEADFACE has access to their API. It's too early to tell if they compromised a password - let's first check if there are any hardcoded secrets in the app.

Your task is to recover the internal API token from the APK. Submit the token as the flag. Example: deadface{2GFEwQvPVIMLJmjGYHgKFWkmpuhrjEnSewMrFRyVMEQ=}

name: Admitted Under Another Name
description:
DEADFACE dumped the patient registry from Aurora Health. Buried in it is one high-profile patient who checked in under a fake name — the staff quietly flagged the record as a VIP. Access the database, find that patient, and report their real Medical Record Number (MRN).

Use the provided MSSQL shell access to query the patients table.

Submit the flag as deadface{MRN}. Example: deadface{AH-1234567}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: Weak RSA
description:
Find the weakness.

The key generation isn't.

Factor n.

name: Web Recon — Read the Headers
description:
📖 Scenario

Web servers communicate more than just the visible webpage.

HTTP response headers can reveal useful information about the server, infrastructure, and security configuration.

🎯 Mission

Inspect the HTTP response headers of:

[Flag1.cgcybercom.online](Flag1.cgcybercom.online)

🎯 Objective

Identify the information exposed through the server's HTTP headers.

Submit only the required answer using the flag format: pcgCTF{answer}

name: Infrastructure — Unsecured Reverse Proxy
description:
📖 Scenario

During your investigation, you discover that the web application is not directly exposed to the backend services.

A reverse proxy is positioned between the public network and an internal service. However, its security configuration may not have been properly hardened.

🎯 Mission

Investigate the infrastructure behind:

Flag.cgcybercom.online

Determine how the reverse proxy communicates with the backend service.

Submit only the required answer using the flag format: pcgCTF{answer}

hints.content: Look beyond the public-facing web application.
Network architecture can sometimes reveal services that aren't directly advertised.
Examine the reverse proxy and determine whether its administrative access has been properly secured.

name: Path Traversal — Off by Slash
description:
📖 Scenario

The web server uses a static resource path to serve files.

Something appears wrong with how the application handles paths. A small difference in how the URL is constructed may allow access outside the intended directory.

🎯 Mission

Investigate:

http://flag.cgcybercom.online

Look for a weakness in the static file path handling.
Submit only the required answer using the flag format: pcgCTF{answer}

name: Live Boot
description:
We think DEADFACE was able to gain a live shell on the device, but the hospital staff insists there is no way to access the device's underlying OS. Somehow, DEADFACE was able to utilize keys for this device that aren't spelled out in the Field Manual.

Access the device's file system and determine what hardcoded keys you can find.

Submit the flag as deadface{flag-text}.

[Access the Device](http://emedra.dctf.io:8080/)

name: The Attending
description:
Stay on the VIP. The patient flagged is_vip = 1 in Aurora's patients table had exactly one inpatient admission in November 2025. We suspect DEADFACE wants to know which physician signed off on that stay — it's the first name in the chain they leaned on. Identify the attending provider for that admission and report their system username.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the username as deadface{username}. Example: deadface{jsmith}.

name: Prying Eyes
description:
Aurora Health logs every time a staff member opens a patient chart. Someone was watching the VIP a little too closely. Find the user account that accessed the VIP patient's chart more times than any other account, and report their username.

You'll need the VIP's MRN first from Admitted Under Another Name. The audit log references patients by that same MRN.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the username as deadface{username}. Example: deadface{jsmith}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: The Original Reading
description:
Aurora Pharmaceuticals ran a Phase III trial for a drug called Veltrexa, and the trial's EDC (electronic data capture) system keeps a full audit trail of every edit in a data_changes table. Most entries are routine source-data corrections — but exactly one rewrote a primary efficacy endpoint, quietly changing the number to make the drug look like it worked. Recover the original value that was overwritten.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the value exactly as it appears in the audit trail, wrapped in the flag. Example: deadface{1.4}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: SQL Skillz
description:
Created By: @G2Gh0st
 
 
For this task, you need to continue your examination of the Aurora Patient Portal application.

After completing Info Leaks and Down the Rabbit Hole, you have collected the patient data that is needed to query the application database file. Use the data collected to determine what medications the current patient is taking other than Ibuprofen.

Submit the result as the flag as deadface{Name}.

name: Diagnosis
Heavy Hand
description:
One Aurora prescriber dispensed far more Schedule II medication than anyone else in the final quarter of 2025 — the classic signature of drug diversion. Using the aurora_pharmacy database, find the prescriber with the highest total quantity of Schedule II medication dispensed between 2025-10-01 and 2025-12-31, and report their DEA number.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the DEA number as deadface{DEA}. Example: deadface{AB1234567}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: Upon the Throne
description:
Pull the threads together. Aurora's breach was not random: an insider clerk snooped a gubernatorial candidate's chart to build kompromat, and a diversion-flagged physician was coerced into faking the Veltrexa trial that would decide a drug's approval. Both insiders were being run by the same DEADFACE handler, whose codename was recovered in a compromised-account field (handler_ref) on each side of the house: the audit-system users and the EHR providers.

Many handler codenames appear across those two tables - around fifteen on each side, so there is no obvious one to guess - but only one appears in both users and providers: the single operative managing an insider on each side. Find that codename.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the codename as deadface{CODENAME}. Example: deadface{JOKER-4}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: After the Lock
description:
Once a clinical trial's database is locked, results are frozen — any edit after the data-lock date is a protocol violation and a fingerprint of tampering. Aurora Health recorded the official lock date for the Veltrexa study right in the studies table. Find the subject whose primary efficacy result (measure = 'primary_efficacy_delta') was modified after the study's data-lock date, and report their subject code.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the subject code as deadface{subject_code}. Example: deadface{ABCD-0101}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: Cereal Killer 04
description:
We have a new set of Spooky Cereals this year, in honor of our New Visitors, who have traveled so long and far to come visit us and to share their other-worldly wisdom with us!

Finally, we have the Greys. Everyone is very familiar with them, primarily because of Hollywood. Big eyes, big bulbous heads with skinny bodies... tiny little mouths and long, spindly fingers. You get the picture.

Unlike the rest of our Far-Flung Friends, the Greys communicate with each other using "Assembly Codes". This has led some to speculate that they are actually biologic meat-puppets that are remotely piloted. Lytton Labs hasn't quite figured out how to talk to them... which is very unfortunate, because they kind of like to ... probe ... their "guests", and they don't seem to pick up on English, such as, "OW, that @#$@#%^^ HURTS!!!"

We have recovered a binary from one of their crashed ships, and we'd like you to analyze it. Once we figure out their favorite spooky cereal, we feel like we can better bond with our new friends!

Submit the answer as deadface{I-For-One-Welcome-Our-New-Buggy-Overlords} ... which is not the REAL FLAG, by the way.

name: Web Recon — Git Repository Leak
description:
📖 Scenario

A developer accidentally deployed a repository directory to the production server.

The repository itself may not be immediately visible through normal browsing. Your task is to determine whether development artifacts have been exposed.

🎯 Mission

Investigate:

[clickThisLink](Flag1.cgcybercom.online/repo/)

Look for the Git repository metadata.

Submit only the required answer using the flag format: pcgCTF{answer}

hints.content: Git repositories contain a hidden directory used to store repository information.
If /repo/ doesn't show it, try requesting the hidden directory directly.

name: Ghost in the Registry
description:
Diverted narcotics need a paper trail that leads nowhere. Investigators suspect a fabricated patient — one who is issued controlled-substance prescriptions but has never actually been seen for a single clinical encounter. Aurora uses one enterprise patient_id across all of its systems, so records join across databases. Find the patient who has at least one Schedule II prescription but zero encounters in aurora_ehr, and report their MRN.

Use provided MySQL shell.

Submit the MRN as deadface{MRN}. Example: deadface{AH-1234567}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: Too Good to be True
description:
The post-lock edit wasn't the only fabrication in the Veltrexa trial. One subject's recorded efficacy improvement is a statistical impossibility — it sits more than three standard deviations above the study-wide mean for the primary endpoint, a telltale sign that a number was invented rather than measured. Identify that outlier subject and report their subject code.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the subject code as deadface{subject_code}. Example: deadface{ABCD-0101}.

[Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: Two Places at Once
description:
Aurora Health's incident-response team knows what DEADFACE did. They still don't know how they got in - until DEADFACE bragged about it. This post surfaced on the GhostTown forum. One legitimate account, used from two places at once. Find the compromised account - the one whose login shows up on two different workstations at the very same timestamp, over and over. Report that account's username.

Use the provided MySQL shell.

Submit the username as deadface{username}. Example: deadface{jsmith}.

[	Access Database](https://aurora.dctf.io/)

name: Who Is Behind the Platform?
description:
Every CTF needs a platform.
But every platform has a story.
You have been given access to a CTF platform. Somewhere within its public traces is the identity of the person who started the project.
Your mission is to uncover the creator.
You are given only the following clues:
Clue 1
The platform is open source.
Clue 2
Its source code contains the history of its development.
Clue 3
The person you're looking for was not merely a contributor — they started the project.
Clue 4
Their name appears in the project's earliest history.

Submit the answer using:
pcgCTF{yourFLAGHEREE.......................}
